newsitem.title: USA: U.S. agency opposes eased species law for flood control. [CORRECTED 01:50 GMT 11/4]
newsitem.headline: U.S. agency opposes eased species law for flood control. [CORRECTED 01:50 GMT 11/4]

text.p: An effort by Republicans to give a blanket waiver for all flood control projects to ignore wildlife protection rules was opposed by the U.S. Interior Department on Thursday.

In the wake of massive floods in California's Central Valley this year, Republican Representative Richard Pombo was pushing a bill that would allow water projects to go ahead without having to comply with endangered species protections.

Water control officials in Pombo, Calif., and farmers (corrects from "Pombo and two geologists") blamed the flooding on the Endangered Species Act, saying levees collapsed because maintenance had been slowed by efforts to protect the elderberry beetle, which was living in bushes on the levee.
"These regulations have been a recipe for disaster. They're an excuse for not getting things done," said Christopher Lee, a trustee for a reclamation district in Walnut Grove, Calif.
Deputy Interior Secretary John Garamendi said huge storms, not the endangered species act, caused this year's disaster.

"The Cosumnes River experienced flows ... twice as high as any recorded flows since before 1906. Clearly, the levee systems were simply overwhelmed by the magnitude of last January's flood," he said in testimony for a House Resources Committee hearing on the bill.
Under existing policies, the government allows emergency work to go ahead to repair levees during disasters without endangered species reviews until after the work is completed.

Garamendi and a California geologist warned the committee that allowing all other flood control work to go on unimpeded would not solve the Central Valley's problems, and could make the area more vulnerable.
The bill "will contribute to a false sense of security and may encourage further development in flood-prone areas, thereby increasing future flood damages," he said.

Flooding in the Central Valley was natural, and efforts to prevent floods in the long run worsened the threat because levees affect underlying river flows, Jeffrey Mount, a geology professor at the University of California in Davis, said.

Environmental critics of the bill called it a thinly veiled attempt by Pombo to gut the Endangered Species Act. Pombo was one of the leaders of the Republican effort in the last Congress to overhaul the law.
